title: The Ant and the Grasshopper
author: Aesop
plot: All summer a grasshopper sings and plays while an ant works hard, carrying food to store for the winter. The grasshopper laughs at the ant for working on such a fine day. When cold winter comes, the grasshopper has no food and is hungry, while the ant is warm and well fed. The grasshopper learns that there is a time for work and a time for play, and that it is wise to prepare for the future.

title: The Fox and the Grapes
author: Aesop
plot: A hungry fox sees a bunch of ripe grapes hanging high on a vine. He jumps again and again, trying to reach them, but they are too high. After many tries he cannot get even one grape. Tired and annoyed, he walks away and tells himself the grapes were probably sour and not worth eating anyway. The fox pretends he never wanted them, showing how people often scorn what they cannot have.

title: The Crow and the Pitcher
author: Aesop
plot: A thirsty crow finds a pitcher with a little water at the bottom, but the neck is too narrow and the water too low for his beak to reach. Instead of giving up, the clever crow picks up small stones one by one and drops them into the pitcher. Slowly the water rises higher and higher until the crow can drink. The story shows that patience and clever thinking can solve a hard problem.

title: The North Wind and the Sun
author: Aesop
plot: The North Wind and the Sun argue about which of them is stronger. They agree that whoever can make a traveler take off his coat is the winner. The North Wind blows hard and cold, but the man only wraps his coat tighter. Then the Sun shines warmly, and soon the man feels hot and takes his coat off himself. The Sun wins, showing that gentle warmth can do what force cannot.

title: The Goose That Laid the Golden Eggs
author: Aesop
plot: A poor farmer discovers that his goose lays one golden egg every day. He sells the eggs and slowly grows rich. But he becomes greedy and impatient, wanting all the gold at once. Thinking the goose must be full of gold inside, he cuts it open, only to find it is just an ordinary goose. Now the goose is gone and there are no more golden eggs. His greed costs him everything.

title: The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse
author: Aesop
plot: A town mouse visits his cousin in the country and finds the simple food plain and boring. He invites the country mouse to the town to taste fine food in a grand house. The country mouse enjoys the feast until a cat and then people burst in, forcing them to run and hide in fear again and again. The country mouse decides he would rather eat simple food in peace than rich food in constant danger, and goes home.

title: The Dog and His Reflection
author: Aesop
plot: A dog is walking home over a bridge with a big bone in his mouth. Looking down into the river, he sees his own reflection and thinks it is another dog with a bigger bone. Wanting that bone too, he snaps at the reflection, and his own bone falls from his mouth into the water and is lost. The greedy dog ends up with nothing, learning that grasping for more can cost you what you already have.

title: The Wolf in Sheep's Clothing
author: Aesop
plot: A hungry wolf wants to catch a sheep but the shepherd guards the flock well. The wolf finds a sheepskin and wears it, walking quietly among the sheep so no one notices him. His trick works for a while as he hides in plain sight. But in the end his disguise leads to his own downfall when he is mistaken for a sheep. The tale warns that a false appearance can hide a dangerous heart.

title: The Milkmaid and Her Pail
author: Aesop
plot: A milkmaid carries a pail of milk on her head to market and daydreams as she walks. She plans to sell the milk, buy eggs, raise chickens, and become rich enough to wear a fine dress and toss her head proudly at the boys. Lost in her dream, she actually tosses her head, and the pail falls, spilling all the milk on the ground. With the milk gone, all her plans are gone too. Do not count on things before they happen.

title: The Bundle of Sticks
author: Aesop
plot: An old farmer has sons who always quarrel with one another. To teach them, he gives them a tied bundle of sticks and asks each to break it, but none can. Then he unties the bundle and gives them the sticks one by one, and each stick breaks easily. He explains that together they are strong like the bundle, but alone they are weak and easy to break. The brothers learn that unity gives them strength.
